A simulator axx makes, or keeps for runs, is not used again after a scenario that put photos in it (its library cannot be emptied); one of yours keeps them

rows.name: documents
rows.takes: files put On My iPhone, in the simulator's Files, before the app starts, where the document picker shows them, for the app to pick, like `documents/safe-place-authorization.pdf` (found as a step finds a file: next to the feature file first; the phone has them by their names). In the picker, tap Browse, then On My iPhone, then the file as a list item, by its name without its extension. The next scenario's reset takes them out again: on a simulator axx makes, On My iPhone is emptied, whatever an app saved there too

rows.name: appium
rows.takes: an Appium server of the project's own or a device farm's, which then runs the device, in place of `device`

rows.name: capability.<name>
rows.takes: an Appium capability for that server, like a device farm's options, as text or JSON

bootTimeout.description: How long a simulator may take to boot, like 30m. The simulator axx sets up once, to clone, takes over ten minutes on GitHub's macOS runners; its clones boot in seconds, and are ready once iOS serves apps' requests for notifications (seconds more, or a minute on a busy Mac). Default 20m.

keep.description: Keep the simulators booted after the run, for the next run to start at once, instead of making them for each run: in Xcode's set, named axx <device type> (n), where Device Hub lists them. Each scenario still has its simulator to itself, and its app reset. A watched run (axx run --watch) keeps them. Default false.

packs.name: desktop-core
packs.doc:
Desktop apps on macOS, Windows and Linux, used as people use them, through the operating system's accessibility tree: what screen readers read. axx starts the app as it ships, with no build for testing, and clicks and types with the pointer and the keyboard, as a person does.

An app is registered for each OS it runs on, by that OS's pack (`desktop-macos`, `desktop-windows`, `desktop-linux`), and every other step is `app-core`'s: a feature lists the app once for each OS and runs unchanged on each. This pack adds what only desktops do: a key pressed, a click at a place on a control, a drag.

**Each scenario has the desktop, and a clean app.** A desktop has one screen, one pointer and one keyboard focus, so on macOS and Windows desktop scenarios take the machine's desktop in turns (other runs on the machine wait too), while other scenarios run alongside them; on Linux, axx runs desktops of its own. Before an app starts in a scenario, its home (a folder of the project's `.axx/desktop`) is emptied, and what its OS keeps of it elsewhere is reset; after the scenario, the app and every process it started are stopped. An app's files are a folder of the files pack whose `owner` is the app: `./` is where its OS keeps an app's data, `~/` its home.

**Screenshots** are of the app's front window, as it draws itself, one for each platform and display scale (`arrivals.darwin@2x.png`). A focused field's text cursor is left out of them, as the web pack leaves it out of its screenshots: it blinks.

params.name: anchor
params.doc: the point of a control that places on it are measured from: its `middle`, or a corner. Places run right and down from it, so one left of or above it is negative
examples: middle
bottom right

steps.expr: the {word} key is pressed in the {word} app
steps.doc: Press a key, with the keys held with it, in the app's focused window: `Enter`, `Escape`, `Tab`, `Control+Shift+S`, as the web pack names them. `ControlOrMeta+Z` is Command on macOS and Control elsewhere, so a feature runs unchanged on each OS.
examples: When the Escape key is pressed in the depot app
When the ControlOrMeta+S key is pressed in the depot app

steps.expr: the {string} {control} in the {word} app is clicked at {int}, {int}
steps.doc: Click at a place on a control, in points from its top left, for what an app draws rather than names: a signature pad, a map, a canvas.
examples: When the "Courier signature" element in the depot app is clicked at 40, 40

steps.expr: the {string} {control} in the {word} app is clicked at {int}, {int} from its {anchor}
steps.doc: Click at a place on a control, in points from its middle or a corner, for what keeps its place there as the control grows with the window or the screen: a picture an app shows in its middle, a button in its bottom right corner. Places run right and down, so one left of or above the point is negative.
examples: When the "Courier signature" element in the depot app is clicked at -40, -20 from its bottom right

steps.expr: the pointer is dragged from {int}, {int} to {int}, {int} on the {string} {control} in the {word} app
steps.doc: Press the pointer at a place on a control, move it to another in steps, as a hand does, and release it there; places are in points from the control's top left.
examples: When the pointer is dragged from 40, 30 to 140, 30 on the "Courier signature" element in the depot app

steps.expr: the pointer is dragged from {int}, {int} to {int}, {int} from the {anchor} of the {string} {control} in the {word} app
steps.doc: Drag on a control as a hand does, with places in points from its middle or a corner, for what keeps its place there as the control grows with the window or the screen. Places run right and down, so one left of or above the point is negative.
examples: When the pointer is dragged from -60, 0 to 60, 0 from the middle of the "Courier signature" element in the depot app

folder.description: The folder of the apps' screenshots, in the project. Unset, each feature keeps its screenshots in a screenshots folder next to its file.

tolerance.description: The share of a screenshot's pixels that may differ (default 0).

update.description: Take every screenshot again, as the app looks now, instead of comparing.

platforms.description: The platforms whose screenshots the project keeps: each compares its own; elsewhere the steps pass without comparing (default: every platform).

traces.description: Which scenarios keep a trace of each app in .axx/desktop/traces: a page with its window after each step, and its controls where the scenario failed (default never).

videos.description: Which scenarios keep a video of their desktop in .axx/desktop/videos, an MP4 file (H.264), and the run one of them all, run.mp4 (default never). OpenH264 Video Codec provided by Cisco Systems, Inc.: axx downloads it from Cisco when a video is first kept; never turns it off.

packs.name: desktop-macos
packs.doc:
macOS apps, through AX, the accessibility tree VoiceOver reads: native apps (AppKit, SwiftUI), web views (Tauri, Wails), Electron, Qt, Java and Flutter, as they ship.

macOS asks that the app running axx be allowed to control the computer: the terminal, the IDE or the CI agent at the top of axx's process tree, in System Settings > Privacy & Security > Accessibility (Device Control & Data Access, on macOS 27), and Screen Recording for screenshots. `axx doctor` checks both, and names the app. Hosted macOS runners allow both already.

**Each scenario has the desktop, and a clean app.** Desktop scenarios take the Mac's desktop in turns: while they run, the screen, the pointer and the keyboard are theirs, so leave the Mac be, or run them in CI. Before the app starts, its home (`HOME` and `CFFIXED_USER_HOME`, which Foundation follows; Java's `user.home`) is emptied, and its preferences, which macOS keeps for the user whatever the home, are emptied too: the domain of the app's bundle identifier, and the domains its registration names (`preferences`: Qt's `QSettings` names its own, after the app's organization). Your own are kept aside during the run and put back when it ends (or as the next run starts, after one that was stopped). Window restoration is off. The keychain is not reset: a sign-in an app keeps there outlives the scenario. An app's `./` files are its home's `Library/Application Support`.

steps.expr: the {word} macos app with the following properties:
steps.doc: Register a macOS app. The app starts when a step launches it. On another OS, the registration does nothing, so a feature registers the app once for each OS it runs on.
examples:
Given the depot macos app with the following properties:
  | app | ../depot-desk/appkit/build/Depot desk.app |

rows.name: app
rows.takes: the app: a `.app` of the project, an installed app's bundle identifier (`com.apple.TextEdit`), or an executable (a file of the project, or a command)

rows.name: args
rows.takes: the arguments it starts with, a quoted one with spaces; a file of the project is relative to axx.yaml

rows.name: env.<name>
rows.takes: an environment variable it starts with, like `env.PARCELS_API`

rows.name: preferences
rows.takes: the preferences domains the app keeps its settings in beyond its bundle identifier's, like `com.parcels-example.Depot desk` (Qt's `QSettings` names its own), separated by commas: emptied before each scenario

rows.takes: its language and region, like `de-DE`

rows.name: timezone
rows.takes: its time zone, like `Europe/Berlin`

rows.takes: `system` for an app the system runs already, like Finder (`com.apple.finder`): the scenario reads it as it runs, and never resets, launches or stops it; the windows it shows during the scenario are closed as the scenario ends

packs.name: desktop-windows
packs.doc:
Windows apps, through UI Automation, the accessibility tree Narrator reads, and the Java Access Bridge for Java apps: native apps (Windows Forms, WPF, WinUI), web views (WebView2: Tauri, Wails), Electron, Qt, Java and Flutter, as they ship.

axx runs apps on the signed-in user's desktop: run it in a terminal there, or as a scheduled task for that user (`schtasks /it`), not as a service or over SSH, which have no desktop. Hosted Windows runners have one. `axx doctor` checks it.

**Each scenario has the desktop, and a clean app.** Desktop scenarios take the machine's desktop in turns: while they run, the screen, the pointer and the keyboard are theirs. Before the app starts, its home is emptied: `USERPROFILE`, and `APPDATA`, `LOCALAPPDATA`, `TEMP` and `TMP` in it, which apps' data folders follow (Java's `user.home` too); the registry keys the registration names are emptied too, your own kept aside during the run and put back when it ends. The profile's own folders, like Documents, are Windows' to resolve, and stay yours. Java apps are read through the Java Access Bridge of the Java that runs them, which axx switches on for the launch. An app's `./` files are its home's `AppData\Roaming`.

steps.expr: the {word} windows app with the following properties:
steps.doc: Register a Windows app. The app starts when a step launches it. On another OS, the registration does nothing, so a feature registers the app once for each OS it runs on.
examples:
Given the depot windows app with the following properties:
  | app      | ..\depot-desk\winforms\bin\Release\net8.0-windows\DepotDesk.exe |
  | registry | Software\Parcels\Depot desk                                       |

rows.name: app
rows.takes: the app: an `.exe` of the project, or a command

rows.name: args
rows.takes: the arguments it starts with, a quoted one with spaces; a file of the project is relative to axx.yaml

rows.name: env.<name>
rows.takes: an environment variable it starts with, like `env.PARCELS_API`

rows.name: registry
rows.takes: the keys under `HKEY_CURRENT_USER` the app keeps its settings in, like `Software\Parcels\Depot desk`, separated by commas: emptied before each scenario

rows.name: locale
rows.takes: its language and region: Windows has none of an app's own, so the machine's apply, and the run says so

rows.name: timezone
rows.takes: its time zone: Windows has none of an app's own, so the machine's applies, and the run says so

rows.name: owner
rows.takes: `system` for an app the system runs already, like File Explorer (`explorer.exe`): the scenario reads it as it runs, and never resets, launches or stops it; the windows it shows during the scenario are closed as the scenario ends

packs.name: desktop-linux
packs.doc:
Linux apps, through AT-SPI, the accessibility tree Orca reads: native apps (GTK 3, GTK 4), web views (WebKitGTK: Tauri, Wails), Electron, Qt, Java and Flutter, as they ship, under X11 or Wayland.

**axx runs desktops of its own**, `desktops` at once (1 by default): each a virtual screen (Xvfb), with its own session bus and accessibility bus for each scenario, and its own view of the file system, in which an app's home is at the same path in every desktop. Nothing shows on your screen, and a feature never names a desktop: a scenario takes one, as a mobile scenario takes a device. It needs Xvfb, dbus-daemon and at-spi2-core (`axx doctor` checks them); more than one desktop needs user and mount namespaces, which a host that forbids them does not give, and then desktop scenarios run one at a time.

**On Wayland** (`display: wayland`), each scenario's desktop is a headless GNOME Shell of its own, the desktop most Linux users run, on the scenario's session bus. Apps start in its GNOME session and pick Wayland or X11 as they do on a GNOME desktop: GTK, Qt 6 and Electron Wayland, Java and Qt 5 its Xwayland (Debian's and Ubuntu's Qt 5 is read on X11 only: with qtwayland5 installed, its registration's `env.QT_QPA_PLATFORM` is `xcb`). The desktop portals answer them as GNOME's do. GNOME Shell's remote desktop takes the pointer's and the keyboard's events, and an extension of axx's, run from the session's folder (nothing is installed), puts each window's frame at the screen's corner, shows no top bar, overview or notification, and takes screenshots. It needs gnome-shell and pipewire (and xwayland, for X11 apps), and a system bus: on a machine with systemd, its logind; in a container without logind, no /run/systemd/seats.

**Each scenario has a desktop, and a clean app.** Before the app starts, its home is emptied, and it starts with `HOME` and the XDG folders in it; the scenario's session bus runs with them too, so the app's settings (dconf), keyring and portals start empty. axx switches on what toolkits need to be read: the assistive technology announcement, the accessibility bus's address on the screen (Qt 5), and java-atk-wrapper for Java apps where it is installed. Chromium (Electron, CEF) builds its tree from the environment, but leaves out what shows: an Electron app's registration starts it with `--force-renderer-accessibility` in its `args`. An app's `./` files are its home's `.local/share`.

steps.expr: the {word} linux app with the following properties:
steps.doc: Register a Linux app. The app starts when a step launches it. On another OS, the registration does nothing, so a feature registers the app once for each OS it runs on.
examples:
Given the depot linux app with the following properties:
  | app | ../depot-desk/tauri/src-tauri/target/release/depot-desk |

rows.name: app
rows.takes: the app: an executable of the project (an AppImage too), or a command on PATH

rows.name: args
rows.takes: the arguments it starts with, a quoted one with spaces; a file of the project is relative to axx.yaml

rows.name: env.<name>
rows.takes: an environment variable it starts with, like `env.PARCELS_API`

rows.name: locale
rows.takes: its language and region, like `de-DE`

rows.name: timezone
rows.takes: its time zone, like `Europe/Berlin`

rows.name: owner
rows.takes: `system` for an app the desktop runs, or starts when another app asks it to, like GNOME Files (`nautilus`): the scenario reads it as it runs, and never resets, launches or stops it

desktops.description: How many Linux desktops run at once: desktop scenarios beyond them wait for one (default 1). More than one needs user and mount namespaces.

display.description: What axx's desktops run: x11, a virtual screen (Xvfb); or wayland, a headless GNOME Shell for each scenario (default x11).

packs.name: models-core
packs.doc:
Stub the models your apps and services run themselves (embedded models): an image classifier on a phone, a model a service loads with ONNX Runtime. A stub is a model in the real one's format, with its inputs and outputs, whose answers are its mappings: the app's runtime loads it as it loads the real model, and an input like one of the mappings' gets that mapping's answer. A stub is a few kilobytes and answers at once, the same every time, where a real model fills a simulator's or an emulator's memory and answers as it likes. Models a service reaches over HTTP are WireMock's: see the model mocks of the WireMock image.

A stub's directory has its model's contract, `contract.json`, what the app relies on from the model: `axx models contract <model>` writes it from the real model, once, and the project keeps it, so no test needs the real model. Its `mappings` folder has the mappings, as WireMock's has its stubs: each JSON file a mapping, or several under `mappings`. A mapping's `input` is a picture (`image`) or a tensor's values (`tensor`), and its `output` the answer, in the terms of the model's task (a classifier's `label` and `score`) or as the outputs' values (`tensors`). An input matches the mapping whose input it is most like, when it is alike enough (the contract's `match.similarity`), and the default mapping (`"default": true`) answers the others.

`axx models build <stub> -o <file>` writes the stub, which the app's test build ships in place of the real model: an Android app's test assets, an iOS app's test target, a service's test image. Stubs are written in the real model's format: ONNX, TFLite (LiteRT), Core ML, ExecuTorch, TensorFlow (SavedModel and TensorFlow.js), Keras, TorchScript, MNN, ncnn, OpenVINO, GGUF (llama.cpp), safetensors (transformers), LiteRT-LM, CTranslate2 (faster-whisper), whisper.cpp and OpenAI Whisper; Tesseract; Piper; and Apple's Foundation Models, whose stub is a Swift type an app's test build gives its sessions. A pack adds formats, tasks and kinds of input of its own: see the stubs guide.

steps.expr: the {word} app's microphone hears the {string} file
steps.doc: The app's microphone hears a recording (a WAV file). Recordings wait, in order, until the app listens: the app's platform speech stub answers the mapping the recording matches (axx matches it as the stub's keys were made), and a web page's own microphone (getUserMedia) records it. The file's name selects no answer.
examples: When the courier app's microphone hears the "recordings/door.wav" file

steps.expr: [[within {duration} ]]the {word} app's speaker plays the {string} file
steps.doc: Check that the app has spoken a recording (a WAV file): an utterance of its speech has the recording's sound. The app speaks with a voice stub, which speaks a mapping's recording for a text that has the mapping's key: the file is the recording the app's words are spoken as. The app's platform pack hears its speech (models-linux: speech-dispatcher's, in the desktops axx runs; models-windows: SAPI's). The check waits for it: 10 seconds, or `within {duration}`.
examples: Then within 10s the depot app's speaker plays the "recordings/handover-rules.wav" file

packs.name: models-ios
packs.doc: Answer supported Speech and Vision calls in debug iOS Simulator apps from prebuilt .axxmodel files in the app's axx-models folder. Speech uses log-mel matching for app-provided audio and the microphone step's precomputed matches for queued recordings. Microphone scenarios feed AVAudioEngine input taps and connections, AVAudioRecorder files (including duration, pause and metering), and AVCaptureSession audio data outputs, then silence. A tap-fed recognition shares its capture's recording and finishes when that recording ends or the app ends audio. Input nodes use 48 kHz mono float PCM independently of the host microphone; taps receive their requested PCM format. Audio data output requires a simulator audio capture device and microphone permission. Foundation Models text sessions, of the system model and of Apple's server model (PrivateCloudComputeLanguageModel; a session of a model of the app's own is left as it is), use the public provider API on iOS 27 or later; a stub whose contract gives format.details.availability (deviceNotEligible, appleIntelligenceNotEnabled or modelNotReady) is an iPhone without the system model, which reports it unavailable. Copy stubs before launching the app; restarting reloads them.

packs.name: models-macos
packs.doc: Answer Mac apps' calls to Apple's models from prebuilt .axxmodel files in the app's axx-models folder (in its `./` files, its home's Library/Application Support): Vision (image classification, text recognition, human and animal rectangles, person segmentation), Speech (SFSpeechRecognizer) and Foundation Models text sessions, of the system model and of Apple's server model (PrivateCloudComputeLanguageModel; a session of a model of the app's own is left as it is), as models-ios does in the iOS Simulator, with the same contracts (`macos.*` APIs). desktop-macos loads axx's library into the app as it starts, from its environment (DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES): macOS lets it into an app signed without the hardened runtime, or with the `com.apple.security.cs.allow-dyld-environment-variables` and `com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation` entitlements (the app's test build's), which axx checks before it starts the app. Speech uses log-mel matching for app-provided audio and the microphone step's precomputed matches for queued recordings; microphone scenarios feed AVAudioEngine input taps and connections, AVAudioRecorder files and AVCaptureSession audio data outputs, then silence (a capture session still opens the Mac's audio capture device, which needs one, and the user's permission to use it). A Mac has no test's grant of speech recognition or the microphone: a stubbed recognizer, and the microphone axx feeds, are authorized. A stub whose contract gives format.details.availability (deviceNotEligible, appleIntelligenceNotEnabled or modelNotReady) is a Mac without the system model, which reports it unavailable. Foundation Models stubs need macOS 27 or later; the rest, macOS 15. Copy stubs before launching the app; restarting reloads them.

packs.name: models-linux
packs.doc: Answer the models Linux apps take from the system, in the desktops desktop-linux runs, from stubs in the app's axx-models folder (in its `./` files, its home's .local/share): Tesseract's language data (a stub of the tesseract format, like `eng.traineddata`), which Tesseract reads from the folder its documented TESSDATA_PREFIX names, and the voice of the desktop's speech service, speech-dispatcher (a Piper voice stub: its `.onnx` and `.onnx.json`), which speaks the app's text with Piper (its `piper` program, on PATH) into the folder the speaker step hears. axx gives the app's speech-dispatcher its user configuration, in the app's home (`.config/speech-dispatcher`): the voice is its only one, and no sound plays (its audio is ALSA's null device, which needs speech-dispatcher's audio plugins). Copy stubs before launching the app; restarting reloads them.

packs.name: models-windows
packs.doc: Answer the models Windows apps take from Windows, from the stubs in the app's axx-models folder (in its `./` files, its home's AppData\Roaming), in the desktops desktop-windows runs: the voice they speak with, SAPI's, from a Piper voice stub, and the Windows AI APIs, from stubs of them. **The voice.** SAPI's (System.Speech's, and native SAPI's), from a Piper voice stub (its `.onnx` and `.onnx.json`). As the app starts, axx adds its voice engine (built with the .NET SDK, 8 or later, into axx's cache) to SAPI's voices, as `axx voice`, makes it the user's default voice, and gives the app the stub: the voice speaks each text with Piper (its Windows release, which axx downloads, pinned) into SAPI's output and into the folder the speaker step hears. SAPI lists the voices in HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Speech\Voices\Tokens only, so axx runs as an administrator, as GitHub's Windows runners do, or as a user who may create keys there; the scenario's end takes the voice out again and puts the user's default voice back. The engine is 64-bit .NET: it speaks in 64-bit apps. **The Windows AI APIs.** The Windows App SDK's: TextRecognizer, ImageDescriptionGenerator, ImageObjectExtractor, and the language model, Phi Silica, with its skills, TextSummarizer, TextRewriter and TextToTableConverter (`windows.ai.*`: `axx models contract` writes their contracts), in a self-contained build (WindowsAppSDKSelfContained), whose own folder has their files, which its manifest maps their classes to. As the app starts, axx puts its library in place of the app's file of each API the folder has a stub of (Microsoft.Windows.AI.Imaging.dll, Microsoft.Windows.AI.Text.dll), and the app's own back as the scenario ends: a class the folder has a stub of is the library's, any other the app's file's; the language model's are the library's together, with a stub of the model or a skill. axx builds the library once for each app, against the app's .winmd files, with C++/WinRT (its release, which axx downloads, pinned) and MSVC (Visual Studio's, or its Build Tools', C++ tools and a Windows 11 SDK). The library answers as Windows does: only an app with package identity whose package declares the systemAIModels capability. A stub of a PC without the model gives the reason (format.details.availability) in Windows' words: NotSupportedOnCurrentSystem, or NotReady, which EnsureReadyAsync makes ready.

packs.name: models-android
packs.doc: Answer SpeechRecognizer, ML Kit built-in image labeling, text recognition, object detection and selfie segmentation, and ML Kit Gemini Nano text generation in debuggable emulator apps from prebuilt .axxmodel files in axx-models. Speech uses log-mel matching for app-provided audio and the microphone step's precomputed matches for queued recordings. Microphone scenarios play recordings into AudioRecord, converted to its rate, channels and PCM format, then silence. MediaRecorder audio capture uses documented JNI registration for its public native controls and public codecs to write the requested file on stop. It supports pause/resume, amplitude, reset/release, paths, File and FileDescriptor outputs, preserving the app's descriptor ownership and microphone permission. It requires the public MediaRecorder(Context) constructor and Java reset/release methods; video, automatic duration/file-size limits and output rotation fail explicitly. The ART agent attaches before application binding. Vision inputs use InputImage.fromBitmap; custom ML Kit model clients retain their native loader. Text generation includes single-chunk streaming through the Prompt API.

packs.name: models-web
packs.doc: Answer a browser's built-in AI (the Prompt API's LanguageModel, Summarizer, Writer, Rewriter, Translator, LanguageDetector, Proofreader) and SpeechRecognition from prebuilt .axxmodel files in the web app's axx-models folder, and play the microphone step's recordings into the page's own microphone (getUserMedia). Copy the files into the app's folder before opening its first page. The adapter runs before the page's scripts, in its frames of its origin and its popups.

packs.name: aws-core
packs.doc:
The AWS account the aws-* packs talk to, set up the way the AWS SDK is set up for the real services.

Register the account once; every aws-* step of the scenario uses it:

```gherkin
Given the parcels aws account with the following properties:
  | region   | eu-west-1             |
  | endpoint | http://localhost:4566 |
```

Without credentials in the table, the SDK finds them as it always does: the `AWS_*` environment variables, the shared files, then the container or instance role. `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL` is honored too, so the same features run against AWS and against an emulator. Values expand `${env:..}` and `${sys:..}`.

steps.expr: the {word} aws account with the following properties:
steps.doc:
Register the AWS account the aws-* steps talk to.

- The first account registered is the default.
- Without `access key id` and `secret access key`, the SDK finds credentials as it always does: the `AWS_*` environment variables, the shared files, then the container or instance role.
- Values expand `${env:..}` and `${sys:..}`, so the same features run against AWS and against an emulator.
examples:
Given the parcels aws account with the following properties:
  | region            | eu-west-1                           |
  | endpoint          | http://localhost:4566               |
  | access key id     | ${env:AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID:-local}     |
  | secret access key | ${env:AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY:-local} |

Given the parcels aws account with the following properties:
  | region  | eu-central-1  |
  | profile | parcels-tests |

rows.name: region
rows.takes: the AWS region, like `eu-west-1`

rows.name: endpoint
rows.takes: where every service of the account is, instead of AWS: a local emulator, like `http://localhost:4566`, where S3 is addressed by path

rows.name: profile
rows.takes: a profile of the shared AWS config and credentials files

rows.name: access key id
rows.takes: the access key ID of static credentials, with `secret access key`

rows.name: secret access key
rows.takes: the secret access key of static credentials, with `access key id`

rows.name: session token
rows.takes: the session token of temporary static credentials

rows.name: asyncapi
rows.takes: an AsyncAPI document, a file of the project or a URL, that the SQS queues and SNS topics follow: every message a scenario sends there, and every message a check finds, is checked against it (with the asyncapi pack)

packs.name: aws-s3
packs.doc:
Upload files to S3 buckets and check the objects your services write there.

The steps use the scenario's AWS account (`the {word} aws account with the following properties:`, from aws-core). Checks wait for the object (10 seconds unless `within {duration}` says otherwise), since services write asynchronously: an upload that triggers processing (an S3 event notification to a queue, say) and the object that processing writes.

steps.expr: the {filepath} file is uploaded to the {word} s3 bucket[[ as {path}]]
steps.doc: Upload a file to the s3 bucket, under the file's name or the name given. Its content type follows the file's extension.
examples: When the invoices/kestrel-2026-09.csv file is uploaded to the carrier-drops s3 bucket
When the invoices/kestrel-2026-09.csv file is uploaded to the carrier-drops s3 bucket as incoming/kestrel-2026-09.csv

steps.expr: [[within {duration} ]]the {word} s3 bucket has a(n) object named {path}
steps.doc: Check that the s3 bucket has an object with that name. The check waits for it: 10 seconds, or `within {duration}`.
examples: Then within 30s the carrier-drops s3 bucket has an object named disputes/kestrel-2026-09.csv

steps.expr: [[within {duration} ]]the {path} object in the {word} s3 bucket is identical to the {filepath} file
steps.doc: Check that the object exists with exactly the content of the file. The check waits for it: 10 seconds, or `within {duration}`.
examples: Then the disputes/kestrel-2026-09.csv object in the carrier-drops s3 bucket is identical to the expected/kestrel-disputes.csv file

steps.expr: [[within {duration} ]]the {path} object in the {word} s3 bucket has the following properties:
steps.doc: Check that the object holds JSON with those values at those paths. The check waits for it: 10 seconds, or `within {duration}`.
examples:
Then the summaries/kestrel-2026-09.json object in the carrier-drops s3 bucket has the following properties:
  | carrier         | KESTREL |
  | lines           | 14      |
  | totals.disputed | 5.25    |

table.note: Each row is a path into the JSON (a property name, a dotted path or a JSONPath) and the value it has there.

steps.expr: [[within {duration} ]]the {path} object in the {word} s3 bucket contains {string}
steps.doc:
Check that the text of the object contains the text.

- The check waits for it: 10 seconds, or `within {duration}`.
- Case matters; runs of spaces and line breaks count as one space.
- The text is read by the object's type: the text of a PDF's pages, the paragraphs and tables of a Word document (.docx), the cells of every sheet of an Excel workbook (.xlsx), the text content (or the markup) of XML and HTML, or the text itself.
examples: Then the invoices/kestrel-2026-09.pdf object in the carrier-drops s3 bucket contains "Total due: 1284.50 EUR"

steps.expr: [[within {duration} ]]the {path} object in the {word} s3 bucket has a row where:
steps.doc:
Check that the table of the object has a row with those values in those columns.

- The check waits for it: 10 seconds, or `within {duration}`.
- The object is a CSV or TSV file, or an Excel workbook (.xlsx; its first sheet), whose first row names the columns.
- A cell is the text the workbook shows, with runs of spaces as one space: a price formatted with two decimals is `"6.90"`, and `""` an empty cell.
examples:
Then within 30s the disputes/kestrel-2026-09.csv object in the carrier-drops s3 bucket has a row where:
  | parcel | PX-5199          |
  | status | UNKNOWN_SHIPMENT |
  | billed | "4.10"           |

table.note: Each row names a column, as the object's first row names it, and the value in that column.

packs.name: aws-sqs
packs.doc:
Send messages to SQS queues and check the messages your services send to them.

The steps use the scenario's AWS account (`the {word} aws account with the following properties:`, from aws-core).

**Checking a queue receives from it**: axx takes each message off the queue, as any consumer would. Check the queues your services **write** to (an outbound queue another system reads); a queue your service consumes is checked by what the service does with the messages. axx starts receiving from the queues a run checks once the services are up, and a check only looks at the messages received since its scenario started. Match on data unique to the scenario: scenarios run in parallel and share the queue.

steps.expr: a message is sent to the {word} sqs queue:
steps.doc: Send a message to the sqs queue; the doc string is its body.
examples:
When a message is sent to the refund-results sqs queue:
  """
  {"claim": "CLM-4106", "status": "PAID", "paidAt": "2026-09-24T10:00:00Z"}
  """

steps.expr: the {filepath} message is sent to the {word} sqs queue[[ with the following attributes:]]
steps.doc: Send a message whose body is the file to the sqs queue, with the attributes of the table when the step has one.
examples: When the messages/refund-failed-clm-4109.json message is sent to the refund-results sqs queue

When the messages/refund-failed-clm-4109.json message is sent to the refund-results sqs queue with the following attributes:
  | failureReason | ACCOUNT_CLOSED |

table.note: Each row is an attribute sent with the message: its name and its value.

steps.expr: [[within {duration} ]]the {word} sqs queue has a message where:
steps.doc:
Check that the sqs queue has a message with those values, received since the scenario started.

- The check waits for it: 10 seconds, or `within {duration}`.
- axx takes the queue's messages off it: check queues your services write to.
examples:
Then within 30s the refund-requests sqs queue has a message where:
  | claim            | CLM-4101 |
  | amount           | 89.5     |
  | attribute reason | DAMAGED  |

table.note: Each row is a path into the message's JSON body (a field name, a dotted path or a JSONPath) and the value it has there. A row `attribute <name>` is instead on the attribute of that name sent with the message, which is text (`"3"` for one that reads as a number), and `undefined` when there is none.

packs.name: aws-sns
packs.doc:
Publish messages to SNS topics and check the messages your services publish.

The steps use the scenario's AWS account (`the {word} aws account with the following properties:`, from aws-core).

**Checking a topic** does not take messages from anyone: for the topics a run checks, axx subscribes a queue of its own (`axx-<run>-<topic>`, with raw message delivery) once the services are up, and removes the subscription and the queue when the run ends. A check only looks at the messages received since its scenario started; match on data unique to the scenario, since scenarios run in parallel.

steps.expr: a message is published to the {word} sns topic:
steps.doc: Send a message to the sns topic; the doc string is its body.
examples:
When a message is published to the parcel-events sns topic:
  """
  {"parcel": "PX-4104", "status": "DELIVERED", "deliveredAt": "2026-09-20T14:05:00Z"}
  """

steps.expr: the {filepath} message is published to the {word} sns topic[[ with the following attributes:]]
steps.doc: Send a message whose body is the file to the sns topic, with the attributes of the table when the step has one.
examples: When the messages/px-4104-delivered.json message is published to the parcel-events sns topic

When the messages/px-4104-delivered.json message is published to the parcel-events sns topic with the following attributes:
  | eventType | ParcelDelivered |

table.note: Each row is an attribute sent with the message: its name and its value.

steps.expr: [[within {duration} ]]the {word} sns topic has a message where:
steps.doc:
Check that the sns topic has a message with those values, received since the scenario started.

- The check waits for it: 10 seconds, or `within {duration}`.
- axx subscribes a queue of its own to the topic for the run.
examples:
Then within 30s the claim-decisions sns topic has a message where:
  | claim               | CLM-4101     |
  | decision            | APPROVED     |
  | attribute eventType | ClaimDecided |

table.note: Each row is a path into the message's JSON body (a field name, a dotted path or a JSONPath) and the value it has there. A row `attribute <name>` is instead on the attribute of that name sent with the message, which is text (`"3"` for one that reads as a number), and `undefined` when there is none.

packs.name: aws-eventbridge
packs.doc:
Put events on EventBridge buses and check the events your services put there.

The steps use the scenario's AWS account (`the {word} aws account with the following properties:`, from aws-core). An event has a detail type, a source and a JSON detail, as in `When a "Damage Reported" event from carrier.kestrel is put on the carrier-events eventbridge bus:` with the detail as the doc string.

**Checking a bus** does not take events from anyone: for the buses a run checks, axx adds a rule of its own (`axx-<run>-<bus>`, matching every event of the account) with a queue of its own as its target once the services are up, and removes both when the run ends. The conditions are paths into the event as EventBridge delivers it: `detail-type`, `source`, and `detail.<field>` for the detail. A check only looks at the events received since its scenario started.

steps.expr: a(n) {string} event from {word} is put on the {word} eventbridge bus:
steps.doc: Put an event with that detail type and source on the bus; the doc string is its detail, in JSON.
examples:
When a "Damage Reported" event from carrier.kestrel is put on the carrier-events eventbridge bus:
  """
  {"parcel": "PX-4105", "carrier": "KESTREL", "note": "Crushed at the depot"}
  """

steps.expr: [[within {duration} ]]the {word} eventbridge bus has an event where:
steps.doc:
Check that the bus has an event with those values, put since the scenario started.

- The check waits for it: 10 seconds, or `within {duration}`.
- axx adds a rule of its own to the bus for the run.
examples:
Then within 30s the parcels eventbridge bus has an event where:
  | detail-type     | Claim Decided  |
  | source          | parcels.claims |
  | detail.claim    | CLM-4101       |
  | detail.decision | APPROVED       |

rows.name: detail-type
rows.takes: the event's detail type, like `Claim Decided`

rows.name: source
rows.takes: the event's source, like `parcels.claims`

rows.name: detail.<field>
rows.takes: a field of the event's detail, or a dotted path into it, like `detail.claim`

table.note: Other paths into the event, as EventBridge delivers it, work too, like `account` or `region`.

packs.name: aws-dynamodb
packs.doc:
Seed DynamoDB tables and check the items your services write.

The steps use the scenario's AWS account (`the {word} aws account with the following properties:`, from aws-core).

A **seed** is a YAML or JSON file that maps table names to the items to put, written as plain JSON (numbers become `N`, objects `M`, arrays `L`):

```yaml
insured-parcels:
  - reference: PX-CLM-1001
    declaredValue: 120
    carrier: KESTREL
```

**Checks** wait (10 seconds unless `within {duration}` says otherwise) until the table has an item, or a number of items, meeting every condition: `attribute | value` rows with a dotted path into maps (`address.city`), and values of their types: a number (`N`) is the number DynamoDB returns (`120`, `49.99`), and a string (`S`) that reads as a number goes in double quotes (`"37073"`). Items are read with a scan, which suits the small tables of a test environment.

steps.expr: a {filepath} dynamodb seed
steps.doc: Put the items of a seed file into their tables: YAML or JSON that maps table names to lists of items. Items are plain JSON: numbers become `N`, objects `M` and arrays `L`.
examples: Given a seeds/insured-parcels.yaml dynamodb seed

steps.expr: [[within {duration} ]]the {word} dynamodb table has an item where:
steps.doc: Check that the table has an item with those values in those attributes. The check waits for it: 10 seconds, or `within {duration}`.
examples:
Then within 30s the claims dynamodb table has an item where:
  | id     | CLM-4101 |
  | status | APPROVED |
  | amount | 89.5     |

table.note: Each row names an attribute of the item, or a dotted path into a map (`address.city`), and the value it has. A number (`N`) is the number DynamoDB returns, like `120` or `49.99`; sets read as lists, and binary as base64.

steps.expr: [[within {duration} ]]the {word} dynamodb table has {int} item(s) where:
steps.doc: Check that exactly that many items of the table have those values in those attributes. The check waits for it: 10 seconds, or `within {duration}`.
examples:
Then the claims dynamodb table has 1 item where:
  | parcel | PX-4107 |

table.note: Each row names an attribute of the item, or a dotted path into a map (`address.city`), and the value it has. A number (`N`) is the number DynamoDB returns, like `120` or `49.99`; sets read as lists, and binary as base64.

packs.name: gcp-core
packs.doc:
The Google Cloud project the gcp-* packs talk to, set up the way the Google Cloud client libraries are set up for the real services.

Register the project once; every gcp-* step of the scenario uses it:


The steps use the scenario's project (`the {word} gcp project with the following properties:`, from gcp-core).

**Checking a topic** does not take messages from anyone: for the topics a run checks, axx creates a subscription of its own (`axx-<run>-<topic>`) once the services are up, and deletes it when the run ends. A check only looks at the messages received since its scenario started; match on data unique to the scenario, since scenarios run in parallel. The conditions are paths into the message data (JSON) and `attribute <name>` rows for its attributes.

  """

steps.expr: [[within {duration} ]]the {word} pubsub topic has a message where:
steps.doc:
Check that the pubsub topic has a message with those values, received since the scenario started.

- The check waits for it: 10 seconds, or `within {duration}`.
- axx creates a subscription of its own to the topic for the run.
examples:
Then within 30s the invoice-events pubsub topic has a message where:
  | attribute eventType | InvoiceReconciled |
  | invoice             | INV-2026-09-KES1  |
  | status              | RECONCILED        |

packs.name: gcp-bigquery
packs.doc:
Seed BigQuery tables and check the rows your services write.

The steps use the scenario's project (`the {word} gcp project with the following properties:`, from gcp-core). Tables are named `dataset.table` (in the project) or `project.dataset.table`.

A **seed** is a YAML or JSON file that maps tables to the rows to insert (a streaming insert, `tabledata.insertAll`):

```yaml
billing.carrier_rates:
  - carrier: KESTREL
    service: express
    price_per_kg: 1.35
```

**Checks** wait (10 seconds unless `within {duration}` says otherwise) until the table has a row, or a number of rows, meeting every condition: `column | value` rows, with a dotted path into `RECORD` columns (`address.city`), and values of their types: an `INT64` is an integer (`2`), a `FLOAT64` a decimal (`2.0`, a whole one too), a `NUMERIC` the number it is (`1.35`), a `TIMESTAMP` in RFC 3339 (`2026-09-24T09:30:00Z`), a `DATE` like `2026-09-24`, and `null` NULL. A check reads the columns its conditions name, of up to 5,000 rows of the table: check the tables your scenarios write, not warehouse-size ones.

steps.expr: a {filepath} bigquery seed
steps.doc: Insert the rows of a seed file into their tables: YAML or JSON that maps tables (`dataset.table` or `project.dataset.table`) to lists of rows. The rows are streamed in (`tabledata.insertAll`).
examples: Given a seeds/carrier-rates.yaml bigquery seed

steps.doc:
Check that the table has a row with those values in those columns.

- The check waits for it: 10 seconds, or `within {duration}`.
- Name the table `dataset.table`, or `project.dataset.table` for another project's.
- An `INT64` is an integer, a `FLOAT64` a decimal, a whole one too (`2.0`), and a `NUMERIC` or `BIGNUMERIC` the number it is (`1.35`); a `TIMESTAMP` is in RFC 3339 (`2026-09-24T09:30:00Z`), a `DATE` like `2026-09-24`, a `DATETIME` like `2026-09-24T09:30:00`, and `BYTES` in base64.
- The check reads only the columns the step names, of up to 5,000 rows.
examples:
Then within 30s the billing.invoice_lines bigquery table has a row where:
  | invoice  | INV-2026-09-KES2 |
  | parcel   | PX-5103          |
  | status   | OVERCHARGED      |
  | billed   | 2.5              |
  | expected | 1.35             |

table.note: Each row names a column, or a dotted path into a `RECORD` column (`address.city`), and the value in it; `null` is NULL.

- The check waits for it: 10 seconds, or `within {duration}`.
- Name the table `dataset.table`, or `project.dataset.table` for another project's.
- An `INT64` is an integer, a `FLOAT64` a decimal, a whole one too (`2.0`), and a `NUMERIC` or `BIGNUMERIC` the number it is (`1.35`); a `TIMESTAMP` is in RFC 3339 (`2026-09-24T09:30:00Z`), a `DATE` like `2026-09-24`, a `DATETIME` like `2026-09-24T09:30:00`, and `BYTES` in base64.
- The check reads only the columns the step names, of up to 5,000 rows.

  | invoice | INV-2026-09-KES1 |
  | status  | MATCHED          |

table.note: Each row names a column, or a dotted path into a `RECORD` column (`address.city`), and the value in it; `null` is NULL.

packs.name: gcp-firestore
packs.doc:
Seed Firestore and check the documents your services write.

The steps use the scenario's project (`the {word} gcp project with the following properties:`, from gcp-core) and its default database.

A **seed** is a YAML or JSON file that maps collections to their documents, by ID (a collection can be nested: `shipments/SHP-1/scans`):

```yaml
shipments:
  SHP-1001:
    carrier: KESTREL
    weightKg: 2.5
    agreedPrice: 3.38
    weighedAt: 2026-09-24T07:40:00Z
    manifest: "2026-09-24"
```

**Dates:** an unquoted YAML date is a Firestore timestamp (`weighedAt` above). A date alone (`2026-09-24`) is midnight UTC. A date and time can have fractional seconds and an offset (`2026-09-24T09:40:00.25+02:00`), and without an offset it is in UTC. A value tagged `!!timestamp` is a timestamp too. Quote a date to keep it a string (`manifest`). JSON has no date type, so the dates of a JSON seed are strings.

**Checks** wait (10 seconds unless `within {duration}` says otherwise): for a document at a path (`invoices/INV-2026-09-KESTREL`) to have properties, or for a collection to have a document meeting every condition. Conditions and properties are `field | value` rows, with a dotted path into maps (`totals.billed`), and values of their types: an integer is `2`, a double `2.0` (a whole one too) and a string `"2"`; timestamps are in RFC 3339 and UTC (`2026-09-24T07:40:00Z`). A collection check reads up to 5,000 of its documents.

steps.expr: a {filepath} firestore seed
steps.doc: Write the documents of a seed file: YAML or JSON that maps collections to their documents, by ID. A number written as an integer (`12`) is stored as an integer, and any other (`12.0`, `2.5`) as a double. Unquoted YAML dates (`2026-09-24`, `2026-09-24T07:40:00Z`) and values tagged `!!timestamp` are stored as timestamps; quote a date to store it as a string.
examples: Given a seeds/shipments.yaml firestore seed

steps.expr: [[within {duration} ]]the {word} firestore document has the following properties:
steps.doc:
Check that the document at that path, like `invoices/INV-2026-09-KES1`, has those values in those fields.

- The check waits for it: 10 seconds, or `within {duration}`.
- A document's integers are integers and its doubles decimals, a whole one too (`6.0`); timestamps are in RFC 3339 and UTC, references their path, bytes base64, and a geo point its `lat` and `lng`.
examples:
Then within 30s the invoices/INV-2026-09-KES1 firestore document has the following properties:
  | status          | RECONCILED |
  | lines           | 2          |
  | totals.billed   | 6.58       |
  | totals.disputed | 0          |

table.note: Each row names a field of the document, or a dotted path into a map (`totals.billed`), and the value it has.

steps.expr: [[within {duration} ]]the {word} firestore collection has a document where:
steps.doc:
Check that the collection has a document with those values in those fields.

- The check waits for it: 10 seconds, or `within {duration}`.
- A document's integers are integers and its doubles decimals, a whole one too (`6.0`); timestamps are in RFC 3339 and UTC, references their path, bytes base64, and a geo point its `lat` and `lng`.
- The check reads up to 5,000 documents of the collection.
examples:
Then the shipments firestore collection has a document where:
  | parcel   | PX-5105 |
  | carrier  | HERON   |
  | weightKg | 3.2     |

table.note: Each row names a field of the document, or a dotted path into a map (`totals.billed`), and the value it has.
